slides.text: She fell into the fjord on the longest night of winter, cracking the sea-ice in a bloom of white steam. By the time the fishermen dragged her ashore in their nets, her celestial fire had faded to a dull, shivering amber. They brought her to my glassworks because my kiln was the only thing on the island hot enough to keep a fallen star from turning to stone.

She lay curled inside my brick furnace, speaking in a language of chiming glass and solar wind. Even with every bellows pumping, my terrestrial coal was too weak; by the third night, frost was creeping across her golden eyelashes. To reignite a star requires the heat of a sun—and the only way to trap that heat was to seal my entire workshop in concave silvered mirrors.

All night I blew and silvered seventy-two curved lenses, encircling the kiln while she watched me with sorrowful, incandescent eyes. 'If I flare, mortal,' she whispered in my mind, 'the light will take your sight.' I adjusted the final mirror and smiled into her fading glow. 'I have spent sixty years looking at glass,' I told her, striking the flint. 'Let the last thing I see be the sky going home.'
